newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa police probe new rightist group over blast.
newsitem.headline: South Africa police probe new rightist group over blast.

text.p: South African police said on Saturday that detectives were probing claims of responsibility by an unknown right-wing group for the Christmas Eve bomb attack that killed four people in a small farming town.

The Boere Attack Troop (BAT) issued an unsigned statement to the national news agency SAPA saying it was behind the blast and threatened further bombings unless a string of demands were met by the state.
"We view this in an extremely serious light and it (the claim) will definitely be thoroughly investigated," police spokesman Captain John Sterrenberg told Reuters.

He said however police were still hunting three fugitive right-wingers who had been convicted of murder in absentia for planting bombs that killed 20 people on the eve of South Africa's historic all-race election in April 1994.

The three men were among four members of the neo-Nazi Afrikaner Resistance Movement (AWB) who escaped from custody in March last year, weeks before their convictions were handed down. A total of nine AWB members were sentenced to 26 years in jail each for the election bombs.
"We're still trying to establish contact with them. They are fugitives from justice in any case, but we also want to discuss the incident at Worcester with them," Sterrenberg said.

The BAT group listed scores of demands in its statement -- addressed to "Mandela, the Communists and all Muslims" -- which included the release of Boer "freedom fighters" from jail, self- rule for Afrikaners, a drastic drop in fuel prices and that the economy be stabilised.

President Nelson Mandela, days before the Worcester blasts, extended the amnesty cut-off date for political crimes to May 10, 1994. The date was originally set as December 1993, which would have excluded the right-wing election bombers.

An adult and three children were killed and about 60 people were wounded when twin pipe bombs exploded at a supermarket and pharmacy on December 24 in Worcester, 90 km (55 miles) northeast of Cape Town. Most of the casualties were blacks or mixed-race.
